vignette:
She still wakes before dawn, the same way she did for fifty years, though now there is no field site to drive to, no data to log. At seventy-seven, Margaret lives alone in a small house at the edge of a town that was once a logging camp. The walls are covered with topographic maps and photographs of rivers, but she cannot look at the one taken in the Klamath Basin—not without her chest tightening. She does not need to see it; she remembers every detail.

The event happened in 1972, when she was a twenty-five-year-old environmental scientist fresh out of graduate school. She had been sent to a remote part of the Pacific Northwest to conduct a vegetation survey for a proposed dam. The work was solitary, and she loved it. On the third night, the camp host—a man in his forties, someone she had exchanged pleasantries with—came to her tent. He did not ask. He did not stop when she said no. She remembers the smell of pine resin and the sound of her own breath. She remembers the weight of him, and the way the tent canvas pressed against her face.

Afterward, she told no one. She finished the survey in four days instead of seven, barely sleeping. She filed her report, which was thorough and correct, and then she requested a transfer to a desk job analyzing water quality samples. She told herself it was a logical career move—more stability, less fieldwork. But she never again spent a night in a tent. She never again camped under the sky.

Margaret’s professional reputation grew. She became known for her meticulous data and her refusal to collaborate with male colleagues after office hours. She never married, never had children. When asked, she would say she was married to her work. And she was. The lab was a fortress: four walls with a lock, predictable instruments, no one who could reach her without permission.

But the fortress had cracks. For decades, she has had nightmares—vivid, recurring scenes of being pinned in a small space. She avoids forests entirely, even now. She lives in a house with no trees close to the windows. She drives only on main roads. When a stranger knocks at her door, she freezes, heart hammering, and waits until they are gone. She has not been to a doctor’s appointment alone in twenty years—a female neighbor drives her.

At work, she became obsessive about safety protocols, especially for young women. She once told a junior scientist, “Never trust a man who offers to help you set up camp.” She did not explain why. She could not.

Now, in retirement, Margaret has more time, and the silence is worse. She cannot ignore the thoughts anymore. She replays that night in loops, trying to find a detail she might have missed—something she could have done differently. She feels guilty for not reporting him, guilty for surviving, guilty for being too afraid to tell her mother. She has not spoken the word “rape” aloud in fifty years. When the news reports a sexual assault, she turns off the television. She has stopped going to the grocery store at night because the parking lot lights make her feel watched.

She did not come to therapy willingly. Her neighbor noticed she had stopped eating properly and made the call. Margaret sat on the edge of the couch, hands clasped, and said, “I don’t know why I’m here. It happened a long time ago.” But her foot was tapping, and her eyes scanned the room for exits. The PCL-5 score of 73 tells a different story than her words. The forest of her own mind is still the place she cannot enter.
